terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, transitive; what one wraps it in, ablative
terms.comment: Wrap a present in paper, a baby in swaddling clothes, the left arm in a cloak. Of a person, sē litterīs involvere, to bury oneself in one’s books (Cicero, below). A wrapper is involūcrum (Traupman 409; see case).

evidence: Plaut. Most. 2.1.77; Cic. Verr. 2.5.72: capite obvolūtō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To cover all over, chiefly of muffling the head (capite obvolūtō) or bandaging a limb (Suet. Dom. 17).

phrases.latin: et pannīs eum involvit, et reclīnāvit eum in praesēpiō
phrases.english: and she wrapped him in swaddling clothes and laid him in a manger

phrases.latin: ubi salūtātiō dēflūxit, litterīs mē involvō, aut scrībō aut legō
phrases.english: once the morning callers have drained away, I wrap myself up in books: I write or I read
Let’s wrap the present in paper.

sources: Lewis & Short: involvo · Lewis & Short: obvolvo · Lewis & Short: involucrum
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 409.
